questions.q: T section: flange 100 mm × 10 mm on top of a web 10 mm × 90 mm. Height of the centroid above the bottom of the web, in mm (1 decimal)?
questions.x: ȳ = ΣA_i y_i / ΣA_i = (1000·95 + 900·45)/1900 = 71.3 mm, so the centroid sits in the web just below the flange.

questions.q: Thin circular ring (tube wall), midline radius R, wall t ≪ R. Second moment of area about a diameter?
questions.x: I = ∫(R sin φ)² R t dφ over 0 to 2π = πR³t, which is half the polar value J = 2πR³t.

questions.q: Complete the principal axes condition
questions.x: The principal axes are where the rotated product of inertia vanishes, which gives |tan 2θ_p| = 2|I_yz|/|I_y − I_z|.

questions.q: Thin semicircular arc, midline radius R, wall t. Second moment of area about the diameter joining its ends?
questions.x: I = ∫(R sin φ)² R t dφ over 0 to π = πR³t/2, exactly half of the full ring value.

questions.q: Bonded strip of equal width: steel layer 10 mm thick (E = 210 GPa) on the bottom, aluminum layer 10 mm thick (E = 70 GPa) on top. Height of the modulus-weighted centroid above the bottom face, in mm?
questions.x: ȳ = ΣE_i A_i y_i / ΣE_i A_i = (210·5 + 70·15)/(280) = 7.5 mm, so the neutral axis moves into the stiffer steel.

questions.q: Rectangle 50 mm wide × 100 mm deep carries N = 100 kN tension and M = 5 kN·m about its strong axis. Maximum normal stress?
questions.x: σ = N/A ± M c/I = 20 ± 60 MPa, so the peak is 80 MPa tension on one face and 40 MPa compression on the other.

questions.q: For a section with I_yz ≠ 0, the neutral axis lies along the applied moment vector only when:
questions.a: The moment acts about a principal axis
w: The section is made of a single uniform material
The applied moment is small compared with yield
The beam is short and deep
questions.x: About a principal axis the bending decouples, so the neutral axis lies along the moment vector; any other orientation tilts it toward the axis of lower bending stiffness.

questions.q: Match each section stiffness (Bauchau and Craig notation, axes x₂, x₃) to its definition
questions.x: With the origin at the modulus-weighted centroid, S, H₂₂, H₃₃ and H₂₃ fully describe extension and bending; H₂₃ = 0 along principal axes of bending.

questions.q: Put the steps for shear flow in a closed single-cell section under a shear load in order
steps: Cut the cell at one point to make it open
Compute the open-section shear flow q_b from the free edge
Add an unknown constant shear flow q₀ around the cell
Find q₀ from moment equilibrium about a point (or zero twist for load through the shear center)
questions.x: The closed shear flow is q = q_b + q₀, and the single extra equation (moment equilibrium or zero twist) fixes q₀.

questions.q: Closed single cell, shear load applied through the shear center. The constant q₀ in the cut cell is found from:
questions.a: Zero twist rate, ∮ q ds/(G t) = 0
w: The free edge condition q = 0 at the cut
Axial force equilibrium of each stringer
Bredt's formula with T = 0 at the root
questions.x: A load through the shear center causes zero twist, and the twist rate is θ' = (1/(2A G)) ∮ q ds/t, so setting it to zero fixes q₀.

questions.q: Two-cell closed section under pure torque T. The extra equation beyond T = 2A₁q₁ + 2A₂q₂ is:
questions.a: Equal twist rate θ' in both cells
w: Equal shear flow in both cells
Zero shear flow in the shared web
Equal shear stress in the outer walls
questions.x: The section rotates as a rigid body in its plane, so every cell has the same θ' = (1/(2A_i G)) ∮ q ds/t.

questions.q: Solid circular shaft, diameter 40 mm, torque 1 kN·m. Maximum shear stress, in MPa?
questions.x: τ_max = T r/J = 16T/(πd³) = 16·10⁶/(π·40³) = 79.6 MPa at the outer surface.

questions.q: Thin rectangular strip, b = 60 mm, t = 3 mm, torque T = 10 N·m. Using J = bt³/3, maximum shear stress in MPa?
questions.x: J = 60·27/3 = 540 mm⁴ and τ_max = G t θ' = T t/J = 3T/(bt²) = 55.6 MPa along the long edges.

questions.q: Complete the twist rate relation
questions.x: Torsional stiffness is GJ, so the twist rate is θ' = T/(GJ) and the total twist of a uniform shaft is TL/(GJ).

questions.q: Saint-Venant torsion of a solid equilateral triangle. Where is the maximum shear stress?
questions.a: At the midpoints of the sides
w: At the three corners of the triangle
At one third of each median
questions.x: The stress function is the product of the three side equations, so shear stress is zero at the corners and centroid and peaks at the side midpoints.

questions.q: Thin-walled open section (an I beam) clamped against warping at one end, torque at the other. Near the clamp, torque is carried mostly by:
w: Bredt-Batho closed-cell shear flow around the section
questions.x: Restrained warping makes the flanges bend in opposite directions, so T = GJθ' − EΓθ''' with the EΓ term dominant near the clamp.

questions.q: In the Galerkin method for a beam ODE L(w) = q, the coefficients come from:
w: Minimizing the integral of the residual squared
Matching the ODE at chosen points
questions.x: Galerkin weights the residual with the trial functions themselves; for self-adjoint problems with admissible functions it reproduces the Ritz equations.

questions.q: Unit load method: in Δ = ∫ M m/(EI) dx, the function m is:
questions.a: Moment from a unit load at the point, along Δ
w: Moment from the real loads per unit length of span
Moment from a unit load at the support
Slope of the real moment diagram
questions.x: Place a unit load at the point, in the direction of the wanted displacement; m(x) is its moment, and a positive Δ is along that unit load.

questions.q: Complete the unit load expression for bending
questions.x: Virtual work gives 1·Δ = ∫ M m/(EI) dx, with M from the real loads and m from the unit load.

questions.q: Linear structure: load P at A gives 2 mm deflection at B (deflections measured along the load directions). The same P applied at B gives deflection at A of:
w: It depends on the stiffness at A
questions.x: Maxwell-Betti reciprocity gives the flexibility matrix symmetric, f_AB = f_BA, so the deflection at A is 2 mm.

questions.q: Clamped-free column (clamped at x = 0), Ritz with w = a x². Ratio of the Ritz P_cr to the exact π²EI/(4L²)? (3 decimals)
questions.x: w = a x² gives P = ∫EI w''² dx / ∫w'² dx = 3EI/L², which is 1.216 times the exact value, an upper bound as Ritz guarantees.

questions.q: Cantilever, length 1000 mm, EI = 10¹¹ N·mm², uniform load 1 N/mm. Tip rotation by the unit (moment) load method, in milliradians?
questions.x: A unit moment at the tip gives m = 1, so θ = ∫ M/(EI) dx = wL³/(6EI) = 1.667 × 10⁻³ rad.

questions.q: Match each column boundary case to a suitable Ritz trial function
pairs: Clamped at x = 0, free at L
Free end value, add ½k w(L)² to U
questions.x: Each function satisfies the essential conditions (w and w' at clamps, w at pins); a spring end leaves w free and enters through its energy.

questions.q: Requiring δW_int = δW_ext for every kinematically admissible virtual displacement is equivalent to:
questions.a: Equilibrium in the domain plus the natural BCs
w: The constitutive law of the material
questions.x: The principle of virtual work is the weak form of equilibrium; integration by parts recovers the field equations and the natural (force) boundary conditions.

questions.q: Put the energy method steps for a rigid-bar stability model in order
steps: Write spring deformations and load-point drop in terms of the DOFs
Form Π = U − PΔ
Set ∂Π/∂θ_i = 0 for the equilibrium paths
Set det of the Hessian ∂²Π/∂θ_i∂θ_j = 0 for P_cr
Use higher derivatives of Π to classify post-buckling
questions.x: The total potential is stationary at equilibrium, and the loss of positive definiteness of its Hessian gives the critical load and mode.

questions.q: Two rigid bars (each L) in a vertical chain: base spring C on θ₁, joint spring energy ½C(θ₂ − θ₁)², dead load P on top. Lowest P_cr?
questions.x: The Hessian is [[2C − PL, −C],[−C, C − PL]], whose determinant gives P = (3 ∓ √5)C/(2L), so the lower root governs.

questions.q: Rigid bar of length L = 500 mm, pinned at the base, horizontal spring k = 2 N/mm at the top that stays horizontal (spring stretch L sin θ), dead load P on top. P_cr in N?
questions.x: U = ½k(L sin θ)² and Δ = L(1 − cos θ) give P_cr = kL = 2·500 = 1000 N.

questions.q: Same two-bar chain as the energy model with C = 1000 N·m, L = 1 m (Hessian [[2C − PL, −C],[−C, C − PL]]). Lowest P_cr in N?
questions.x: P_cr = (3 − √5)C/(2L) = 0.382·1000 = 382 N, with the mode having θ₂ larger than θ₁.

questions.q: Complete the Southwell plot statement
questions.text: Plotting δ/P against δ gives a straight line of slope ___
questions.x: From δ = δ₀ (P/P_cr)/(1 − P/P_cr), δ/P = δ/P_cr + δ₀/P_cr, so the slope is 1/P_cr and the intercept is δ₀/P_cr.

questions.q: Koiter form P/P_cr = 1 + aξ + bξ² near bifurcation. The structure is imperfection sensitive when:
w: b > 0 for any value of a
a and b are both strictly positive
questions.x: Imperfection sensitivity follows a falling branch: asymmetric (a ≠ 0) or unstable symmetric (a = 0, b < 0) bifurcation.

questions.q: Beck's column (cantilever with a tangential follower tip load) loses stability by:
questions.x: The follower load is nonconservative, and the kinetic method gives coalescing frequencies (flutter) at P ≈ 20.05 EI/L².

questions.q: For a conservative system, the static (adjacent equilibrium) and kinetic (vibration) methods give:
w: A lower load from the kinetic method
A lower load from the static method
Loads that differ by the mass ratio
questions.x: For conservative loads, the lowest natural frequency goes to zero exactly at the static bifurcation load.

questions.q: Planar beam: fixed at A, rollers at B and C, all in-plane reactions counted. Degree of static indeterminacy?
questions.x: Reactions are 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 and a planar body has 3 equilibrium equations, so the degree is 5 − 3 = 2.

questions.q: In the force (flexibility) method, after removing the redundants the released structure must be:
w: A mechanism with one free DOF
questions.x: The released (primary) structure is stable and determinate, so its deflections at the redundant locations follow from equilibrium and standard formulas.

questions.q: Match each case to its standard deflection
questions.x: These four results plus PL³/(48EI) for a central point load cover most superposition problems on the board.

questions.q: Simply supported beam, central point load P. Midspan deflection?
questions.x: Each half acts as a cantilever of length L/2 with tip load P/2, giving (P/2)(L/2)³/(3EI) = PL³/(48EI).

questions.q: Propped cantilever: fixed at A, roller at B, span L, point load P = 16 kN at midspan. Roller reaction at B, in kN?
questions.x: Compatibility: P(L/2)²(3L − L/2)/(6EI) = R L³/(3EI) gives R = 5P/16 = 5 kN.

questions.q: Fixed-fixed beam, central point load P. Magnitudes of the end moment and midspan moment?
questions.x: Symmetry and zero end slopes give end moments PL/8 hogging; the free moment PL/4 minus PL/8 leaves PL/8 sagging at midspan.

questions.q: A beam rests on a linear spring support of stiffness k with reaction R. The compatibility condition there is:
w: Spring force = k times beam slope
questions.x: The spring compresses by R/k, so the beam deflection at the support equals R/k in the direction of spring compression.

questions.q: Complete the equivalent spring of a simply supported beam at midspan
questions.x: Midspan deflection under P is PL³/(48EI), so the beam acts as a spring k = 48EI/L³ at that point.

questions.q: Equivalent spring of a fixed-fixed beam for a point load at midspan?
questions.x: Fixed-fixed midspan deflection is PL³/(192EI), four times stiffer than the simply supported beam.

questions.q: Rotational stiffness of a cantilever tip for an applied tip moment (M per unit tip rotation)?
questions.x: A tip moment gives uniform curvature M/(EI), so the tip rotation is ML/(EI) and k_θ = EI/L.

questions.q: Cantilever, L = 2000 mm, EI = 10¹² N·mm², tip also supported by a spring k = 125 N/mm to ground. Tip load 10 kN. Tip deflection in mm?
questions.x: The beam acts as k_b = 3EI/L³ = 375 N/mm in parallel with the spring, so δ = 10000/(375 + 125) = 20 mm.

questions.q: Two springs k₁ and k₂ connected in series carry a load. They share:
questions.a: The same force, and deflections add
w: The same deflection, and forces add
questions.x: Series springs carry one force and add flexibilities, 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂; parallel springs share one deflection and add stiffnesses.

questions.q: Wing strut: E = 70 GPa, A = 200 mm², length 2000 mm, at 30° to the wing. Vertical stiffness it adds at its wing attachment (wing vertical motion only), in N/mm?
questions.x: Strut axial stiffness EA/L = 7000 N/mm projects as (EA/L) sin²α = 7000·0.25 = 1750 N/mm vertically.

questions.q: Cantilever with its tip on a spring k under uniform load. Which limit checks confirm the answer?
questions.a: k → 0: free cantilever; k → ∞: propped cantilever
w: k → 0: fixed-fixed beam; k → ∞: a free cantilever
k → ∞ gives a simply supported beam
questions.x: R = (wL⁴/(8EI))/(L³/(3EI) + 1/k) goes to zero as k → 0 and to the propped cantilever value 3wL/8 as k → ∞.

questions.q: Put the force method steps in order
steps: Find the degree of indeterminacy
Choose redundants and release them
Compute released deflections at the redundants by superposition
Write compatibility, including R/k terms at springs
Solve for the redundants and back-substitute
questions.x: The force method trades the unknown redundants for compatibility equations, one per redundant.

questions.q: Complete the fixed-fixed beam result under uniform load w
questions.x: End moments are wL²/12 hogging, and the free moment wL²/8 minus wL²/12 leaves wL²/24 sagging at midspan.

questions.q: Complete the thin curved beam bending energy (arc angle θ, radius R)
questions.x: For a thin curved beam, arc length ds = R dθ, so the bending energy is U = ∫ M² R dθ/(2EI).

questions.q: Quarter ring, radius R, clamped at one end, tip load P along the radius toward the center. Tip deflection along P?
questions.x: With the angle φ measured from the free end, M = PR sin φ and δ = (1/EI)∫PR² sin²φ R dφ over 0 to π/2 = πPR³/(4EI).

questions.q: Quarter ring as above (clamped at one end, tip load toward the center): P = 100 N, R = 200 mm, EI = 10⁸ N·mm². Tip deflection along the load in mm?
A closed ring under a diametral pair of loads P. Why is an extra equation needed?
w: The loads are self-equilibrated, so U = 0
The ring is a mechanism under symmetric loads
Shear energy dominates in a closed ring
questions.x: Symmetry leaves an unknown moment M₀ at the cut section, and least work ∂U/∂M₀ = 0 gives M₀ = PR(1/2 − 1/π) with M = PR/π under the loads.

questions.q: Thick curved beam (R/h small) in bending. The normal stress through the depth is:
questions.a: Hyperbolic, NA shifted toward the center
w: Linear, with the neutral axis at the centroid
Parabolic, NA at the outer fiber
questions.x: Winkler theory gives σ ∝ y/(R_n − y), a hyperbolic distribution with the neutral axis shifted toward the center of curvature and peak stress on the inner fiber.

questions.q: At a rigid joint in a frame, compatibility requires:
questions.a: Equal rotation of all members at the joint
w: Zero moment in every member at the joint
Equal axial force in all members at the joint
questions.x: A rigid joint keeps the angles between members, so all member ends rotate together and the member end moments balance any couple applied at the joint.

questions.q: L frame: vertical column of height h = 1000 mm clamped at its base, rigid joint at the top, horizontal arm L = 1000 mm, vertical load P = 1000 N at the arm tip, EI = 10¹¹ N·mm² for both. Vertical tip deflection (bending only) in mm?
questions.x: δ = PL³/(3EI) + PL²h/(EI) = 3.33 + 10.0 = 13.33 mm, the second term from the column rotation under the constant moment PL.

questions.q: In a frame of slender members, axial strain energy N²L/(2EA) is usually small compared with bending because:
questions.a: Bending energy exceeds axial by about (L/r)²
w: Axial forces vanish at rigid joints of a frame
EA is smaller than EI for slender members
Axial energy cancels between the members
questions.x: For a slender member, bending flexibility L³/EI exceeds axial flexibility L/EA by a factor about (L/r)², so bending dominates.

questions.q: In a sandwich beam, the load-carrying roles are:
questions.a: Faces carry bending, core carries shear
w: Core carries bending, faces carry shear
Both carry bending in proportion to E
Faces carry shear, core carries axial load
questions.x: The stiff thin faces form a couple that resists moment, and the light core spaces them apart and carries transverse shear.

questions.q: Sandwich beam, width b, face thickness t (thin), face centroid separation d, face modulus E_f. Bending stiffness?
questions.x: Two faces at ±d/2 give D = 2 E_f b t (d/2)² = E_f b t d²/2, neglecting the faces' own small bending stiffness and the core.

questions.q: Complete the transformed section rule (reference material 1)
questions.text: Width of material 2 in the transformed section = n b, with n = ___
questions.x: Scaling the width by n = E₂/E₁ keeps the force and moment of material 2 at the same strain, and stress in it is σ₂ = n σ_transformed.

questions.q: Steel rod (EA = 20 MN) bonded inside an aluminum tube (EA = 70 MN), equal lengths, axial load 90 kN on rigid end plates. Load in the steel rod, in kN?
questions.x: Both share one strain ε = P/ΣEA = 90 kN/90 MN, so the steel carries 20/90 of the load, 20 kN.

questions.q: A steel plate is bonded to the bottom of a homogeneous timber beam. The neutral axis moves:
w: Toward the top of the timber
It stays at the timber centroid
questions.x: The neutral axis passes through the modulus-weighted centroid, which shifts toward the stiffer steel.

questions.q: Match each thin ring case (bending only) to its result
pairs: Quarter ring, tip load toward center
Quarter ring, tip load along the tip tangent
Full ring, diametral loads: diameter change
Full ring, diametral loads: moment under P
questions.x: All four follow from U = ∫M²R dθ/(2EI) with Castigliano, and least work for the closed ring's unknown moment.

questions.q: Put the Castigliano steps for a curved cantilever in order
steps: Cut at angle φ and draw the free body to the tip
Write M(φ) from the tip loads
Form U = ∫M² R dφ/(2EI)
Differentiate δ = ∂U/∂P (add a dummy load if needed)
questions.x: Castigliano's second theorem turns the moment function into a displacement along the chosen load.

questions.q: Two bonded materials under axial load P (rigid end plates, perfect bond). They share:
w: The same stress, σ = P/ΣA_i, in both
questions.x: Compatibility forces one strain, so each material carries force E_iA_i ε, in proportion to its axial stiffness.

questions.q: Complete the governing equation of a uniform column under axial compression P
questions.x: Equilibrium of a deflected element gives EI w'''' + P w'' = 0, with general solution A sin kx + B cos kx + Cx + D, k² = P/(EI).

questions.q: Complete the n-th buckling load of a pinned-pinned column
questions.x: Pinned ends give sin kL = 0, so kL = nπ and P_n = n²π²EI/L²; the second mode needs four times the first load.

questions.q: Match each end condition to its boundary conditions (axial load P)
questions.x: The free end has zero moment and zero transverse shear including the axial load's component, EI w''' + P w' = 0.

questions.q: Pinned-pinned aluminum column: E = 70 GPa, solid circle diameter 40 mm, L = 1 m. Euler load in kN (1 decimal)?
questions.x: I = πd⁴/64 = 1.257×10⁵ mm⁴ and P_cr = π²EI/L² = 86.8 kN.

questions.q: The Johnson parabola is used for columns with slenderness:
w: Above √(2π²E/σ_y), in the elastic range only
Any value, as a safety factor
questions.x: Below the transition slenderness the Euler stress exceeds σ_y/2, so the Johnson parabola σ_cr = σ_y − (σ_y²/(4π²E))(KL/r)² governs.

questions.q: Transition slenderness √(2π²E/σ_y) between Johnson and Euler for E = 200 GPa, σ_y = 250 MPa?
questions.x: √(2π²·200000/250) = 125.7; at this slenderness both curves give σ_cr = σ_y/2.

questions.q: Pinned column with initial bow w₀ sin(πx/L) under P < P_cr. Total midspan deflection?
questions.x: The bow is amplified by 1/(1 − P/P_cr), so deflection grows without bound as P approaches P_cr.

questions.q: Pinned column, initial midspan bow 2 mm (half-sine), load P = 0.75 P_cr. Total midspan deflection in mm?
Pinned column, load P at eccentricity e, c = extreme fiber distance, r = radius of gyration. Secant formula for σ_max?
questions.x: The eccentric beam-column has midspan moment Pe sec(kL/2) with k = √(P/EI), which gives the secant formula.

questions.q: The Southwell plot is useful in column tests because it:
questions.a: Gives P_cr from pre-buckling data, any w₀
w: Gives the post-buckling curvature coefficient b
questions.x: Plotting δ/P against δ gives a line of slope 1/P_cr whose intercept is δ₀/P_cr, so tests stay well below collapse.

questions.q: For an unstable symmetric bifurcation with an imperfection, the limit load P_max is found by:
questions.a: Setting dP/dξ = 0 on the imperfect path
w: Setting P = P_cr in the perfect path
Setting the imperfection amplitude to zero
Equating U to the work of P
questions.x: The imperfect path has a maximum; solving dP/dξ = 0 there gives P_max/P_cr ≈ 1 − c ε^(2/3), the two-thirds power law.

questions.q: A stable symmetric system (like the Euler column) with a small imperfection follows a path that:
questions.a: Rises smoothly past P_cr with no maximum
w: Peaks below P_cr, then drops away
Stays at zero deflection until P reaches P_cr
questions.x: Stable symmetric systems are imperfection insensitive: deflection grows rapidly near P_cr and the load keeps rising.

questions.q: Pinned column of length L on a stiff Winkler foundation of modulus k. The critical mode number n satisfies roughly:
w: (nπ/L)² ≈ k/EI, so the first mode governs
questions.x: P_n = EI(nπ/L)² + k(L/nπ)² is minimized near (nπ/L)⁴ = k/EI, so a stiff foundation selects short waves with P_cr ≈ 2√(kEI).

questions.q: A slender column switches from mild steel to high-strength steel with the same E. Its elastic buckling load:
questions.a: Stays the same, since it depends on EI
w: Falls, since the alloy is more brittle
questions.x: Elastic buckling is a stiffness limit set by EI and L, while yielding is a strength limit set by σ_y.

questions.q: Put the Euler column derivation steps in order
steps: Draw the deflected column and cut it: M = −P w (pinned ends)
Write EI w'' + P w = 0 with k² = P/(EI)
Use w = A sin kx + B cos kx
Apply w(0) = w(L) = 0, giving B = 0 and sin kL = 0
Take kL = π for P_cr = π²EI/L²
questions.x: The nontrivial solution exists only at the eigenvalues kL = nπ, and the lowest gives the Euler load.

questions.q: Ritz with w = a sin(πx/L) for a uniform pinned-pinned column gives:
questions.x: The trial function equals the exact buckled shape, so the Rayleigh quotient ∫EI w''² dx/∫w'² dx gives exactly π²EI/L².

boards.prompt: Here is a Z section with a vertical load. Find the principal axes and the neutral axis, and give me the peak bending stress. Now add an axial tension: where does the neutral axis go?
points: Locate the centroid, compute I_y, I_z, I_yz, and get the principal angle from |tan 2θ_p| = 2|I_yz|/|I_y − I_z|
Resolve the moment onto the principal axes and superpose the two principal bending stresses
The neutral axis is the line σ = 0 and tilts toward the axis of smaller principal stiffness
Peak stress is at the point farthest from the neutral axis
Axial tension adds a uniform N/A, which shifts the neutral axis parallel to itself away from the centroid

boards.prompt: Sketch a sandwich beam with thin faces and a soft core. Write the bending stiffness, then tell me why Euler-Bernoulli overpredicts its stiffness and how Timoshenko fixes it.
points: Bending stiffness is dominated by the faces, D ≈ E_f b t d²/2 with d the distance between face centroids
The core carries the transverse shear, with shear stiffness about G_c b d
Timoshenko theory adds a shear strain γ, so deflection = bending part + shear part (PL/(kGA) for a cantilever)
The shear correction factor k is 5/6 for a solid rectangle
Shear deformation matters for low core G, short spans and high modes

boards.prompt: Three thin walls meet at a junction in a box beam. How do the shear flows relate there? Now give me the full shear flow in a single-cell box under a vertical shear offset from the shear center.
points: Longitudinal equilibrium of the junction gives Σq_in = Σq_out
Cut the cell, compute q_b = −(V/I)∫y t ds from the cut, then add q₀
Find q₀ from moment equilibrium of the shear flows about a convenient point
The offset load creates a torque about the shear center, adding uniform shear flow T/(2A)
The twist rate follows from θ' = (1/(2AG))∮ q ds/t

boards.prompt: Compare the torsion of a solid ellipse, an equilateral triangle and a thin strip. Where does the peak stress occur in each, and which analogy helps you see it?
points: The Prandtl stress function satisfies ∇²ψ = −2Gθ' with ψ = 0 on the boundary
For the ellipse (semi-axes a > b), the peak shear stress is at the ends of the minor axis, τ = 2T/(πab²)
For the equilateral triangle, the peak is at the side midpoints, with zero stress at corners and centroid
For a thin strip, J ≈ bt³/3 and τ_max = 3T/(bt²) along the long sides
The membrane analogy shows peak stress where the membrane slope is steepest, near the closest boundary points

boards.prompt: A quarter circular ring is clamped at one end with a radial load at the tip. Get the tip deflection along the load, then tell me how you would get the deflection perpendicular to it.
points: Use thin curved beam energy U = ∫ M²/(2EI) R dφ
With the clamp at φ = π/2 and the load P toward the center at the tip, M = PR sin φ
δ = ∂U/∂P = πPR³/(4EI) along the load
For the perpendicular displacement, add a dummy load Q there, differentiate with respect to Q, then set Q = 0
The unit load method gives the same result with m from a unit load in the wanted direction

boards.prompt: Explain Maxwell-Betti reciprocity and prove it from energy. Then use Ritz with one term to estimate a column's buckling load and tell me whether it is high or low.
points: Apply P₁ then P₂ and the reverse; equal total work gives P₁ δ₁₂ = P₂ δ₂₁
The flexibility and stiffness matrices are symmetric
Ritz: choose admissible w = a φ(x), set ∂Π/∂a = 0 with Π = ½∫EI w''² dx − ½P∫w'² dx
P_Ritz = ∫EI φ''² dx / ∫φ'² dx is an upper bound on P_cr
Adding terms lowers the estimate toward the exact value

boards.prompt: Here is a rigid bar on a pin with a horizontal translational spring at the top. Find P_cr with energy and classify the post-buckling path. Now let the spring stay attached to a fixed wall so it rotates: what changes?
points: Π = ½k(L sin θ)² − PL(1 − cos θ)
Equilibrium: θ = 0 or P = kL cos θ, and P_cr = kL
P falls with θ, so the bifurcation is unstable symmetric and imperfection sensitive
Load reduction for an imperfection scales as ε^(2/3)
A wall-anchored spring stretches L sin θ + O(θ⁴), so P_cr = kL and the path stays unstable symmetric; an inclined spring adds a θ³ term in Π and makes the bifurcation asymmetric

boards.prompt: A column carries a tangential follower load. Why does the static method fail, what do you use instead, and what does the Southwell plot give you in a test of a conservative column?
points: Follower loads are nonconservative, so equilibrium can stay unique while the system goes unstable
The kinetic method tracks the natural frequencies as P increases
Instability is flutter, when two frequencies coalesce; Beck's column gives P ≈ 20.05 EI/L²
For a conservative imperfect column, δ/P versus δ is a line of slope 1/P_cr
Southwell extracts P_cr from pre-buckling data without knowing the imperfection

boards.prompt: Here is a cantilever whose tip sits on a spring k, with a uniform load. Find the spring force, then check your answer in the limits.
points: Degree of indeterminacy is one; choose the spring force R as the redundant
Compatibility: wL⁴/(8EI) − RL³/(3EI) = R/k
k → 0 gives R → 0, the free cantilever
k → ∞ gives R = 3wL/8, the propped cantilever

boards.prompt: A wing is braced by a strut at an angle. Model the strut as a spring on the wing and find the strut force for a uniform lift. What if the strut is very soft or very stiff?
points: The strut acts as a vertical spring k = (EA/L_s) sin²α at its attachment
Take the strut vertical component as the redundant and write wing deflection there = R/k
Strut axial force = R/sin α
Soft strut gives the free cantilever wing; stiff strut gives a wing propped at the attachment
The strut also puts axial compression into the wing spar, which matters for buckling

boards.prompt: Find the end moments of a fixed-fixed beam under uniform load by superposition. Then tell me the equivalent spring of this beam at midspan, and compare it with a simply supported and a cantilever beam.
points: Release the end rotations, then restore zero end slopes with end moments
End moments are wL²/12 hogging and midspan moment wL²/24 sagging
Midspan point stiffness of the fixed-fixed beam is 192EI/L³
Simply supported midspan stiffness is 48EI/L³ and cantilever tip stiffness is 3EI/L³
Each extra end restraint raises the point stiffness

boards.prompt: Explain how you choose redundants for a continuous beam over three supports. Does the choice change the answer? Now one support settles by Δ: how do you include it?
points: Any set of redundants that leaves a stable determinate structure is valid
The final reactions and moments are unique, independent of the choice
Good choices give simple released-structure deflections (internal moments at supports are common)
A settlement enters the compatibility equation as a prescribed displacement Δ at that redundant
Settlement moments scale with EI, unlike load moments

boards.prompt: Here is a quarter circular ring clamped at the top, free end at the side, with a load at the tip. State your load direction, then derive the tip deflection along it. Now give me the deflection perpendicular to the load.
points: Take φ from the free end; the radial load P toward the center gives M = PR sin φ
U = ∫ M² R dφ/(2EI) over 0 to π/2 and δ = ∂U/∂P = πPR³/(4EI)
For the perpendicular (tangential) deflection, add a dummy tangential load Q, with M = PR sin φ + QR(1 − cos φ)
∂U/∂Q at Q = 0 gives a perpendicular deflection of magnitude PR³/(2EI)
A tangential tip load alone gives (3π − 8)PR³/(4EI) along itself

boards.prompt: A thin ring is squeezed by two opposite loads P. Find the moment distribution and the change of diameter along the loads.
points: By symmetry, analyze a quarter with unknown moment M₀ at the section 90° from the load
M(θ) = M₀ − (PR/2)(1 − cos θ) and least work ∂U/∂M₀ = 0 gives M₀ = PR(1/2 − 1/π)
The moment under the load has magnitude PR/π
The diameter along the loads shortens by (π² − 8)PR³/(4πEI) ≈ 0.149 PR³/EI
The diameter perpendicular to the loads lengthens

boards.prompt: Design a sandwich panel for bending. Which part does what, how do you get the stiffness, and what failure modes worry you?
points: Faces carry the bending as a couple, D ≈ E_f b t d²/2
The core carries transverse shear, with shear stiffness about G_c b d
Deflection = bending part + core shear part, so a Timoshenko type model is used
Separating the faces raises D with d² at little weight
Watch face yielding, face wrinkling, core shear failure and debonding

boards.prompt: A beam is made of aluminum with a steel strip bonded to it. Find the neutral axis and the stresses. Then the same two materials form a bar under axial load: how is the load shared?
points: Transform to one material with n = E₂/E₁ applied to widths
The neutral axis is at the modulus-weighted centroid, ∫E y dA = 0
Stress in material i is σ_i = E_i κ y, with κ = M/ΣE_iI_i about that axis
Under axial load both materials share one strain ε = P/ΣE_iA_i
Each carries force in proportion to E_iA_i

boards.prompt: Derive the Euler load from the fourth-order equation. Now clamp one end and leave the other free: what are the boundary conditions and the effective length?
points: EI w'''' + P w'' = 0 with w = A sin kx + B cos kx + Cx + D, k² = P/(EI)
Pinned ends give sin kL = 0 and P_cr = π²EI/L²
Clamped end: w = w' = 0; free end: w'' = 0 and EI w''' + P w' = 0
Clamped-free gives cos kL = 0, so P_cr = π²EI/(4L²) and K = 2
Effective length KL is the distance between inflection points of the mode, extended past a free end where needed (2L for clamped-free)

boards.prompt: Your column has an initial bow. Show me how the deflection grows with load and how you would get P_cr from a test. Then put the load at an eccentricity.
points: With w₀ sin(πx/L), the total deflection is w₀/(1 − P/P_cr)
Southwell: δ/P versus δ is a straight line of slope 1/P_cr
An eccentric load gives midspan moment Pe sec(kL/2), leading to the secant formula
Both imperfections make deflection rise rapidly as P approaches P_cr
Failure then comes from yielding at the extreme fiber under combined P/A and bending

boards.prompt: Short columns yield, long ones buckle. Sketch σ_cr versus slenderness, and tell me where Johnson applies. Now set the column on an elastic foundation: which mode governs?
points: Euler: σ_cr = π²E/(KL/r)², a stiffness limit
Johnson parabola σ_cr = σ_y − (σ_y²/(4π²E))(KL/r)² applies below √(2π²E/σ_y)
The curves meet tangentially at σ_y/2
On a foundation, P_n = EI(nπ/L)² + k(L/nπ)², so stiff foundations select higher modes
The critical load approaches 2√(kEI)

boards.prompt: Use energy and Ritz to estimate a column's buckling load. When is your answer exact, and how do imperfections change things for stable versus unstable systems?
points: Π = ½∫EI w''² dx − ½P∫w'² dx, with an admissible trial function
The Rayleigh quotient gives an upper bound, exact when the trial function is the true mode
w = a sin(πx/L) is exact for the uniform pinned column
Stable symmetric systems are imperfection insensitive and keep gaining load
Unstable symmetric systems peak at P_max/P_cr ≈ 1 − c ε^(2/3), from dP/dξ = 0
